opus-5.5.text:
I think people tend to underestimate how much of the difference between models comes from data selection rather than raw data access. If you look at the big labs, the pool of available data is actually more similar than people assume. Everyone has access to roughly the same public web crawl, the same books, code repositories, and academic papers. There are some differences at the margins: one company might have a particular licensing deal, or proprietary data from its own products. But the foundation is largely shared.

Where things really diverge is in what you do with that data. How do you filter it? How do you deduplicate it? How do you decide what quality means for a given document? And then, crucially, how do you mix it? What proportion of code versus math versus conversational text versus multilingual content? Those decisions have an enormous effect on the capabilities that emerge, and they're surprisingly hard to get right. Small changes in the mixture can shift a model's reasoning ability or its factual reliability in ways you wouldn't predict up front.

So I'd say selection and curation are probably the bigger lever today. Having unique data sources matters, especially as the public web gets more saturated and more of it becomes model-generated. But a team that is very disciplined about data quality, that runs careful ablations and really understands how each slice of data contributes, can often get more out of the same raw material than a team with more data but less rigor.

That's also why so much of the work has shifted toward things like synthetic data and post-training data. That's where you have the most control. You can design data that targets exactly the capability you want, rather than hoping it emerges from the general distribution. Over time I expect the competitive edge to come less from "who has the most data" and more from "who understands their data best."

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I think it's one where the conventional wisdom has shifted a lot over the past few years.

Early on, the assumption was that the big differentiator would be who has access to proprietary data. If you own a search engine or a social network or a huge codebase, you have this moat that nobody else can replicate. And there's some truth to that, but I think it turned out to matter less than people expected, at least for pretraining. Most of the frontier labs are drawing from broadly similar pools: the public web, books, code, academic papers. The raw sources overlap enormously.

Where I've seen the real leverage is in selection and curation. Two teams can start from essentially the same crawl and end up with very different models depending on how they filter, deduplicate, weight domains, and decide what to upsample or throw away. Quality filtering alone can be worth more than a several-fold increase in raw data volume. And it compounds, because the choices you make about data mixture interact with everything downstream, from how the model reasons to what it hallucinates.

The other thing I'd point out is that "data sources" is becoming a less static concept. Synthetic data, model-generated rationales, data distilled from stronger models, human feedback loops, all of that means the dataset is increasingly something you build rather than something you find. So the question shifts from "what do you have access to" toward "how good is your judgment about what to generate and keep."

That said, I don't want to say sources are irrelevant. For specialized domains, or for post-training where you need high-quality expert demonstrations, access really does matter. If you can get a thousand examples of genuine expert reasoning in some narrow field, that can be worth more than a million generic ones. But at the scale of general-purpose models, I'd put more weight on the taste and infrastructure around selection than on who holds which exclusive corpus.

astra-6.text:
I think selecting the data is often more important than simply having access to a different source. There’s a lot of overlap in the data available to different companies, but you can get very different results depending on what you choose to train on and how you mix it together.

More data isn’t necessarily better. You want to think about quality, diversity, duplication, and what capabilities you’re trying to teach the model. A dataset might be useful for learning facts, but less useful for learning how to reason through a problem or follow instructions. And filtering too aggressively can remove unusual examples that are actually valuable.

So I’d frame it as a selection and experimentation problem. You train on different mixtures, evaluate what improves, and use that feedback to refine the data. Unique sources can certainly help, particularly for specialized tasks, but access alone doesn’t tell you how much value you’ll get out of them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think selecting the data is at least as important as having access to different sources. You can have a huge amount of data, but that doesn’t mean every piece of it is going to help the model. You have to think about quality, diversity, and what you want the model to learn.

A lot of companies have access to overlapping public data. The difference is often in what they do with it: how they filter it, remove duplicates, and balance different types of content. Even with the same starting material, those choices can produce quite different results.

Unique data can certainly be valuable, especially for specialized tasks. But I wouldn’t look just at how much proprietary data a company has. I’d also look at whether they can identify which data actually improves the model, and use experiments to keep refining that selection.
